title: Bhagats in kirtan
hook: their hymns are sung like any other Gurbani

segments.voice: Yesterday, weaver, shoemaker, barber, king: the Bhagats' trades read like a street, and your line was the whole street. Today, that street starts to sing.

The harmonium is already breathing when the door opens. Three ragis sit on the low platform, one at the tabla. The room is half full: a grandmother with a bag of fruit, two teenagers near the back, a man straight from a night shift. One shabad ends, the tabla settles, and a new one begins. Same raag, same melody family, same heads bowed. Nobody stops to ask who wrote it. But glance at the heading, and the name isn't a Guru's. It's Kabir's.
screen: `THE HARMONIUM IS ALREADY PLAYING.` → `A NEW SHABAD BEGINS.` → `THE HEADING SAYS KABIR.`

segments.voice: The Granth is arranged by raag, the musical mode a hymn is meant to be sung in: Asa, Gauri, Sorath, Dhanasri. When the Gurus' hymns in a raag are done, the Bhagats' hymns follow in that same raag. Kabir in Gauri. Ravidas in Gauri too. Farid in Asa, as we saw a few weeks back. No appendix at the back: they live in the same rooms as the Gurus' words, set to the same music. Each Bhagat hymn has a heading with its raag and the Bhagat's name, often with ji added, a word of respect. That small mark tells the singer what to sing and the listener whose voice is speaking. It doesn't tell anyone to sing it differently. So a ragi can move from a hymn of Guru Arjan straight into one of Namdev, and the tabla doesn't change its manners. The Rahao line, the pause line at the hymn's center, is sung as the refrain, the same way. When the shabad ends, people bow the same way. Sikhs call the hymns of the Granth bani, or gurbani, the Guru's word. The Bhagats' hymns are also called bhagat bani, which names whose voice it is, but they're read and sung as part of the Guru, not as quotations borrowed from outside. A Sikh singing Kabir isn't stepping out of the Guru's house. The whole book is the house. That's why the Bhagats are hard to spot in a gurdwara: their place is marked by a name, not a separate stage.
screen: `THE GRANTH IS ARRANGED BY RAAG.` · `BHAGAT HYMNS SIT IN THE SAME RAAGS.` · `THE HEADING NAMES THE VOICE.` · `SUNG AND BOWED TO THE SAME WAY.` · then, large: `ALL GURBANI.`

segments.voice: If you have a recording of a Bhagat's shabad, play it now and listen once, all the way through, before checking whose it is. If not, carry one Bhagat line from these weeks in your own words, Parmanand's question, what did all that hearing change, or Surdas's line about the company you keep, and let it ride the breath the way a refrain comes back in kirtan. If you pray, Waheguru can ride the breath instead.
Kirtan. Singing the hymns of the Granth with music: the Bhagats' hymns sung, heard and bowed to the same way as the Gurus' own.
Your line: all gurbani. The heading names the voice; the singing doesn't change. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In gurdwaras, ragis sing the Bhagats' shabads in kirtan alongside the Gurus' hymns, in the raag the Granth assigns them, and the congregation listens and bows in the same way.

chat.says: When Sikhs sing Kabir's hymns in the gurdwara, is that different from singing the Gurus'?
options: No. Same raag, same refrain, same bow; the heading just names whose voice it is.
Yes. Bhagat hymns are sung in a plainer style, kept apart from the Gurus' music.
Yes. They're only read aloud at the end, after the Gurus' hymns are sung.
chat.meaning: The Bhagats' hymns sit in the same raags as the Gurus' and are sung and bowed to the same way, as part of gurbani.

raag.meaning: the musical mode a hymn is meant to be sung in

Rahao.meaning: the pause line at a hymn's center, sung as the refrain

gurbani.meaning: the Guru's word: the hymns of the Granth

ragi.meaning: a musician who sings the Granth's hymns in kirtan

Kabir.meaning: a weaver-poet whose hymns are in the Granth

notes: Structural claim: within each raag, the Bhagats' hymns follow the Gurus' hymns. Confirm this is fair to state generally (some exceptions may exist, e.g. saloks at the end of the Granth).
Examples of Kabir and Ravidas hymns in Gauri, and Farid in Asa (day 762): confirm.
Headings marked 'ji' (e.g. 'Bhagat Kabir ji'): confirm phrasing is fair.
'Bhagat bani' as a common term for the Bhagats' compositions: confirm.
